stem: Which equation has an energy change that is equal to the first ionisation energy of bromine?

options.B: Br(g) → Br⁻(g) – e⁻
options.C: ½Br₂(g) → Br⁺(g) + e⁻
options.D: ½Br₂(g) → Br⁻(g) – e⁻

stem: Why is the first ionisation energy of phosphorus greater than the first ionisation energy of silicon?

options.A: A phosphorus atom has one more proton in its nucleus.
options.B: The atomic radius of a phosphorus atom is greater.
options.C: The outer electron in a phosphorus atom is more shielded.
options.D: The outer electron in a phosphorus atom is paired.

stem:
T is an element in Period 3.
The first ionisation energy of T is lower than that of the element with one less proton.
The oxide of T does not react with water.
What is the identity of T?

options.B: silicon
options.C: sodium
options.D: sulfur

stem: Which factor causes helium to have a higher first ionisation energy than hydrogen?

options.A: In the 1s orbital in helium, electrons are paired.
options.B: The lowest energy level in helium is filled.
options.C: The nuclear charge in helium is higher than in hydrogen.
options.D: There is less shielding of the outer shell in helium.

stem: Why is the second ionisation energy of sodium larger than the second ionisation energy of magnesium?

options.A: The attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron is greater in Na⁺ than in Mg⁺.
options.B: The nuclear charge of Na⁺ is greater than that of Mg⁺.
options.C: The outer electron of Na⁺ is more shielded than the outer electron of Mg⁺.
options.D: The outer electron of Na is in the same orbital as the outer electron of Mg.

stem: Which statement gives the correct definition of the first ionisation energy of an element?

options.A: The energy released when one electron is removed from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms.
options.B: The energy required to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous $1+$ ions.
options.C: The energy required to remove one electron from one mole of atoms of the element.
options.D: The energy required to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of the element in its standard state.

stem: The first ionisation energy of an element is 1251 kJ mol$^{-1}$. Calculate the energy, in units of $10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$, needed to remove one electron from a single gaseous atom of this element. Use $N_A = 6.02\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}$.
Which equation represents the third ionisation energy of aluminium?
An element X has $IE_1$ of 740 kJ mol$^{-1}$ and $IE_2$ of 1630 kJ mol$^{-1}$. Calculate the energy, in kJ, needed to convert one mole of gaseous X atoms into one mole of gaseous $\ce{X^2+}$ ions.
Which equation represents the first ionisation energy of magnesium?
Which statement best describes the variation of first ionisation energy across Period 3 from sodium to argon?

options.A: It increases generally, with a small decrease from silicon to phosphorus and a small decrease from sulfur to chlorine.
options.B: It increases generally, with a small decrease from magnesium to aluminium and a small decrease from phosphorus to sulfur.
options.C: It increases steadily with no decreases at all.
options.D: It decreases generally, with small increases at magnesium and phosphorus.

stem: First ionisation energy decreases from beryllium to barium. Which statement explains this?

options.A: The nuclear charge increases and the shielding stays the same, so the attraction to the outer electron falls.
options.B: The outer electron is in a shell further from the nucleus and is shielded by more inner shells, so it is less strongly attracted.
options.C: The nuclear charge decreases down the group, so the attraction to the outer electron falls.
options.D: The atoms have more electrons, so the repulsion between electrons in the outer shell increases.

stem: Why does each successive ionisation energy of an element increase?

options.A: Electrons removed from a positive ion are always taken from a lower shell.
options.B: After each electron is removed the remaining electrons are drawn closer to the same nuclear charge, with less electron repulsion, so they are held more strongly.
options.C: Each time an electron is removed the nuclear charge increases by one, so the attraction increases.
options.D: The electron being removed has to overcome the repulsion of the electron already removed.

stem: For the element aluminium, which pair of successive ionisation energies has the largest difference between them?

options.B: first and second
options.C: second and third
options.D: fourth and fifth

stem: Why is energy needed to remove an electron from a gaseous atom?

options.A: The electron is attracted to the other electrons in the atom.
options.B: The negative electron is attracted to the positive nucleus.
options.C: The negative electron is repelled by the positive nucleus.
options.D: The electron is held in place by the neutrons.

stem: Which change would increase the attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron of an atom?

options.B: More protons in the nucleus with the outer electron in the same shell.
options.C: Adding an extra inner shell of electrons.
options.D: The outer electron moving to a shell further from the nucleus.

stem: Which statement about the first ionisation energy of an atom is correct?

options.A: It depends only on the number of protons in the nucleus.
options.B: It depends on the strength of attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron.
options.C: It depends on how strongly the outer electron is attracted to the inner electrons.
options.D: It depends only on the number of electrons in the outer shell.

stem: The first ionisation energy of oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen. Which statement explains this?

options.A: Oxygen has more shielding by inner shells than nitrogen.
options.B: Two of the oxygen 2p electrons are paired in one orbital, and the repulsion between them makes one easier to remove.
options.C: Oxygen has a lower nuclear charge than nitrogen.
options.D: The half-filled 2p subshell in nitrogen is more stable, so it has a lower energy.

stem: The first ionisation energy of sodium is much lower than that of neon. Which statement explains this?

options.A: The outer electron in sodium is in a $2p$ orbital.
options.B: The outer electron of sodium is in a new shell further from the nucleus and is shielded by more inner electrons.
options.C: Sodium has a greater nuclear charge than neon.
options.D: The atomic radius of sodium is smaller than that of neon.
